story_text.value:
Pintura is designed for AI agents to work on plaintext files and for humans to review in a browser.

The premise is that when you're doing slides with AI agents, you mainly need to review their work and iterate until you're happy.

The main benefits are: 1. You can use git for version control and clear diffs. 2. The browser UI is designed for review: flip between versions with visual changes highlighted, pin comments, or drag/reword directly. 3. Your agent gets a CLI that helps it catch things like text overflow, misaligned elements, hanging words, etc.

It pairs with our spreadsheet companion Libreta (github.com/editide/libreta) if you want to link numbers. Clicking a linked number on a slide pops up a spreadsheet showing the formula or a screenshot of the original source.

I've been using this to build financial decks from the terminal with Claude Code (and now Antigravity). It's much nicer than flipping back and forth between Excel and PowerPoint. Here are some decks I've built with this setup: https://iterativaresearch.com/

Everything (preview, checks, screenshots, HTML/PDF export) is Apache-2.0 and runs locally with no account. PowerPoint export currently runs through our API with a free plan.

story_text.value:
I'm between jobs right now, and I'm bad at sitting idle. I could have built yet another portfolio site with a chatbot and a smiling robot avatar, but I wanted to spend the time on something people might actually use.

There was a second reason. My feed is full of stories about LLM agents that burn thousands of dollars in tokens overnight. I suspected that most of them say more about the process than about the tools, and I wanted to check that on real work.

So over about three weeks, with Claude Code on a $20/month Pro plan as the main tool (plus $100 of promotional credits that were expiring anyway, and some free-tier model sessions for the routine parts), I ported four native libraries to fully managed C#, with no P/Invoke and no native binaries:

- Leptonica.Managed - Leptonica 1.87.0, image processing and the base of Tesseract OCR; about 2,700 functions. https://github.com/sensboston/Leptonica.Managed - Stb.Managed - seven of Sean Barrett's stb libraries (image load/save, resize, TrueType, rect_pack, DXT, Perlin). https://github.com/sensboston/Stb.Managed - MetadataSharp - EXIF/MakerNotes, IPTC, XMP and ICC read/write. Not a port: written from the specs, with Exiv2 as the reference. https://github.com/sensboston/MetadataSharp - MdfLibrary.Managed - mdflib, the ASAM MDF format of automotive data loggers, with the same API as its Windows-only C++/CLI wrapper, plus a cross-platform viewer with live CAN capture. https://github.com/sensboston/mdflib.net

All four are on NuGet under MIT.

I wouldn't call this vibe coding. The model wrote most of the code, but the work went the way any port of this size should go, with or without an LLM. First we discussed the architecture: what maps to what in C#, what stays bit-exact and what may be optimized, what is ported and what is left out. Then came a written plan in stages, each with a measurable exit condition. Before the first line of the port, the native library was built and became the oracle; the tests compare against it, not against the model's opinion of what the output should be. Then the work went in small batches, each merged only when CI was green.

The checks are boring on purpose: pixel by pixel against Leptonica's golden files, byte by byte against stb, tag by tag against exiv2 on its own test corpus, file by file against the native MdfLibrary. Parsers are fuzzed. It still isn't bulletproof: the GPU path of Stb.Managed passed every test on ILGPU's CPU accelerator and did not work at all on a real CUDA card. Tests are only as honest as the hardware they run on.

One result surprised me: the managed code is faster than C on most operations - about 1.3-2.0x single-threaded for Leptonica (regular Release build of the C library) and 1.5-1.8x for stb (-O3 -march=native). The JIT emits Vector128/256/512 code for the actual CPU, and Leptonica's C code has almost no SIMD. It is not faster everywhere: stb's hand-written SIMD resize still wins on one core, and JPEG on ARM64 is slower. The slow cases are listed in each repo.

Total extra cost beyond the subscription: $0. The expensive part was waiting for usage limits to reset; my patience turned out to be the scarcest resource in the project.

Happy to answer questions about the process, the verification, or the parts that went wrong.

story_text.value:
We built Hyper Elements. A open source content engine for agents. It lets them build emails, PDFs or images in React using much fewer tokens.

The agent writes content, our engine handles the layout and markup. It also tells the agent what the problems are in the content and how to fix them.

We tested it by giving Claude Code a brief and run it 5 times with different libraries like Hyper Elements, React Email and MJML. Each run, Hyper Elements used fewer tokens and produced a passing email much faster. The benchmark is also open source in the repo.

story_text.value:
tl;dr: We just open-sourced Wakeshift, which lets any MCP server serve interoperable events via MCP Events or harness-specific bridges. This allows MCP servers to push events to harnesses that don't support MCP Events today, including Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.

Hi folks! The MCP Events spec was approved and merged five days ago, allowing MCP servers to emit events directly to agent subscribers. (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol...) This allows MCP developers to push events directly to agents for long-running tasks (e.g. CI, crawls, starting agents) or external actions (e.g. emails, human approvals, alerts).

However, the catch is that support for MCP Events is very light. Claude Code and Codex don't support it at all, and most of the implementations support the draft version rather than the merged spec. Many harnesses can work around this with plugins or hooks, but every MCP server has to build it for each harness.

Wakeshift provides interoperable events to your MCP server. You call emit() and Wakeshift pushes the event to each subscribed agent in whatever format they accept: per the MCP Events final spec, an earlier draft, or through a hook / plugin where needed. If the harness requires a hook / plugin and it's not already installed, the agent will be notified and receive instructions on how to install it for the user.

Additionally, the MCP Events spec defines three delivery mechanisms: webhook, push (via held HTTP request) and pull (via HTTP polling). The Wakeshift SDK serves push and poll from your MCP server, so agents that can't accept inbound HTTP webhooks (e.g. most agents running on laptops) can still get events within seconds.

Subscriptions only start when an agent calls a tool that subscribes it, and users can list or stop them anytime. Some harnesses can only be woken by putting a message into the conversation, so Wakeshift wraps the content as an external event to reduce the risk of prompt injection.

The repo linked has a quickstart guide to get this working locally in a few minutes. Or you can try our hosted webhook service to test it yourself without an installation. (https://try.wakeshift.ai)

We'd love feedback, PRs for harnesses we don't cover, reports when it doesn't work. As you can imagine, there's a combinatorial explosion of servers, harnesses, models, OSs, etc. so we expect there to be some rough edges. Are there any MCP servers you're using that you think could benefit from having events today?

title.value: Show HN: Wakeshift – Open-Source MCP Events for Claude Code, Codex and More

story_text.value:
I am in the industry for 15+ years, studied CS, and actually, never really "liked" programming. It was a means to an end. I have written about programming (and published books), so don't get me wrong: I like the craft and I miss the sense of accomplishment after hours and days of struggling and fixing a problem with 2 lines of code.

What I see in my personal spending and habits: I get free tokens from my company, and I spent between 3k-5k a month at the start of the year. Models got cheaper, but also: The usefullness ran its course a little bit for me.

I still don't write code by hand, but when doing research, finding solutions, even some decisions (using Opus 5.5 and Astra 6.2 for example) are more and more questionable. I handed large research tasks to models, but even small questions like: "What do you think about these PR comments pointing out issues" (I need to be vague, working for a larger company), it didn't find even basic facts I found via Google and reading the docs for 2mins.

I usually did higher level thinking, researched with the model, and then went to the implementation phase. But lately, I am not happy with both the research results (I continuesly have to narrow it down, go back, refine... I spend a day or 2 days refining, which in the end, I can do by myself now and actually feel a sense of accomplishment). Even the implementation isn't all that great.

Maybe my bar for acceptable work is higher now, since these tools are not "magic" anymore. I think I gave them more leeway in the beginning because they wowed me. But now... not so much anymore. I even dread opening up Claude Code or Codex and I'd rather read and write code myself, and just give them smaller tasks, or once I nailed it down, I let a large chunk of code write by a model (because it "types" faster...).

Am I alone? I read a lot of think pieces, I have agents working on my private dedicated server to maintain my machine and set up my self-hosting services. But more and more, I'd rather.... do it myself again, be more precise, and use it as a workhorse instead of a thinking researcher.

title.value: Ask HN: Am I the only one whose AI hype is cooling down a lot?

story_text.value:
joonoo.art turns one photo into a comic book (or picture book) starring the people in it. Upload a photo of up to four people, say who's who, pick a story or write your own, choose a style, and in under a minute you see the cover and the story. The preview is free with no account. You pay only if you want the full book: starts at $4.99 for a PDF, or about $25 printed before shipping.

Hi HN, I'm Saro, a granddad and CTO (formerly chief architect of Fidelity NetBenefits, and head of engineering at IDEMIA for TSA PreCheck).

Reading picture books with my granddaughter last summer, I had the inspiration. I wanted her to be the hero of one.

I launched it in August 2025 and got some orders and happy customers, but I held back on promoting it. The hard part was keeping the same face on every page. The models would hallucinate extra fingers or a different child halfway through, and vision models couldn't reliably catch it. Testing was almost entirely manual, so every small change took days.

What changed in 2026 is that Claude Code got good at writing and running test plans, and its built-in browser can now do much of the visual QA on the artwork. It continues to be challenging to make sure that people's body types, facial features, and costumes remain consistent to the story and the book, but with the ability to do testing on a large scale, I have been able to improve the quality sufficiently to please most of the audience.

I am beyond excited to see what parents and grandparents are creating for their kids - from superboys to dragon-riding to dollhouses that come alive, these kids have wonderful surprises waiting for them under the tree. Even grown-ups seem to be having fun with it.

AI art raises fair questions. We label every book as AI-made and never imitate living artists, and I've written about what we owe artists and authors: joonoo.art/blog/what-we-owe-artists-and-authors

The question I'd most like this crowd's view on: how would you test image consistency at scale - when there are demands in so many different directions that could not have been anticipated or tested? Particularly when you're supporting many languages and selling in many countries?

title.value: Show HN: Keeping faces and features consistent across 24 AI-driven comic pages

story_text.value:
Whenever Claude hands a step back to me, a signup, onboarding or an API key Im lost; and most of the time stuck. No context, stuck on something easy. Me and Claude have switched seats quite fast: claude does the work and I'm the one who needs to be told what to do.

And speed matters now. I have Claude Code sessions running all day, so I made one shortcut. Control-Option-A sends the window I'm looking at to a session and the answer shows up next to my work. I use it for everything now, not just the steps Claude gives me. Reading something, on X, on YouTube, one shortcut and I get an answer.

Right now is Mac & Claude Code only, free and open source. A few days old so things might break.

PS: I know Anthropic might build something similar but I wanted to share it because I spend most of my day in it now

story_text.value:
I love to fiddle with a logic game when I have some time to kill, but these days half the playtime is long non-skippable ads.

The concept is simple, in the game you turn lasers and mirrors in order to reach all the crystals. It starts out simple, but later new mechanics are introduced, like splitters, portals and linked grids and at this point, random tapping is far from enough to succeed. If the early levels aren’t fun, try and skip ahead and see if you feel more of a challenge. Especially in Master

I recently added a progression system with achievements and cosmetic skins, to make the player experience more rewarding and fun

The levels are created procedurally with a generator and filtered by a set of rules and conditions, the levels are picked by an agent judge panel and then finally reviewed by me before being put into the game. This was honestly the most challenging part to get correct, and there’s still room for improvement.

AI disclosure: the code is written with Claude Code, and I’ve used ChatGPT’s image generator for concept art. The music is created on ElevenLabs.

Does it feel fun to play? Is it too easy or difficult? Does the progression and reward system actually feel rewarding?

Hope you’ll give it a try. Enjoy!

title.value: Show HN: I built a laser puzzle game because I was tired of constant ads
